stem: A postpartum client has heavy bleeding and a soft, boggy uterus. The nurse begins fundal massage. Which technique is appropriate?

options.A: Stabilize the lower uterine segment near the symphysis pubis with one hand while using the other to firmly massage the fundus.
options.B: Place both hands over the fundus and apply firm downward pressure until the uterus moves lower in the pelvis and feels smaller.
options.C: Support the fundus with one hand while using the other to massage the lower uterine segment just above the symphysis pubis.
options.D: Pause the massage when uterotonic therapy starts and reassess the fundus after the medication has been given before resuming massage.

rationale: Fundal massage for postpartum uterine atony is performed with one hand on the fundus while the other supports the lower uterine segment near the symphysis pubis; firm fundal massage stimulates uterine contraction and the lower-segment support helps prevent uterine inversion. B omits lower-segment support and adds unsupported downward displacement of the uterus. C reverses the therapeutic roles of the hands because the fundus is massaged while the lower uterine segment is supported. D incorrectly makes massage sequential with uterotonic treatment; the 2025 WHO postpartum-haemorrhage guideline recommends uterine massage as part of the rapid first-response treatment bundle alongside uterotonic therapy and other indicated interventions.
educational_objective: For uterine atony with postpartum bleeding, stabilize the lower uterine segment near the symphysis pubis with one hand and firmly massage the fundus with the other while the broader postpartum-haemorrhage response proceeds concurrently.
source_organization: Open Resources for Nursing / NCBI Bookshelf; World Health Organization
source_document_title: Nursing Health Promotion — Postpartum Care; Consolidated guidelines for the prevention, diagnosis and treatment of postpartum haemorrhage
source_version_date: NCBI Nursing Health Promotion current edition accessed 2026-08-25; WHO consolidated postpartum-haemorrhage guideline 2025
source_locator: NCBI Bookshelf, Nursing Health Promotion > Postpartum Care > Fundal Massage: place one hand on the fundus while the other supports the lower uterine segment near the symphysis pubis to prevent uterine inversion; apply firm pressure to the fundus to induce contraction. WHO 2025 Consolidated PPH Guideline > Recommendation 26, Uterine massage for the treatment of postpartum haemorrhage: uterine massage is recommended for PPH and should start once PPH is diagnosed as part of the first-response treatment bundle; Recommendation 29 describes rapid uterine massage with an oxytocic agent, tranexamic acid, IV fluids, genital-tract examination, and escalation of care.
source_claim_supported: Appropriate fundal massage uses one hand to support the lower uterine segment near the symphysis pubis while the other massages the fundus, and therapeutic uterine massage is integrated into immediate treatment of postpartum haemorrhage rather than delayed until after uterotonics.

supporting_sources.document_title: Consolidated guidelines for the prevention, diagnosis and treatment of postpartum haemorrhage
supporting_sources.locator: Recommendation 26, Uterine massage for the treatment of postpartum haemorrhage; Recommendation 29, first-response treatment bundle for postpartum haemorrhage.
supporting_sources.claim_supported: Uterine massage is recommended once postpartum haemorrhage is diagnosed and is part of a rapid first-response bundle rather than a measure deferred until uterotonic therapy is completed.

blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Physiological Adaptation, printed p. 47: apply knowledge of nursing procedures, pathophysiology and psychomotor skills when caring for a client with an alteration in body systems; provide care for clients experiencing complications of pregnancy/labor and/or delivery, including hemorrhage.
blueprint_topic: Physiological Adaptation — immediate nursing intervention for postpartum haemorrhage due to uterine atony
correction_summary: Rebuilt the distractors to remove absolute-word cueing and replace crude errors with realistic technique and sequencing mistakes. The corrected item preserves one directly sourced fundal-massage technique and distinguishes it from unsafe hand placement, unsupported downward pressure, and inappropriate delay during the postpartum-haemorrhage response.

audit_findings.clinical_category: Postpartum haemorrhage — uterine atony and fundal massage technique
audit_findings.stem: PASS — heavy bleeding plus a soft boggy uterus gives a coherent uterine-atony scenario and asks one psychomotor-priority question.
audit_findings.option_A: PASS — directly matches the NCBI-described two-hand fundal-massage technique and is uniquely appropriate.
audit_findings.option_B: PASS as distractor — uses a plausible two-hand maneuver but omits lower-segment stabilization and adds unsupported downward pressure.
audit_findings.option_C: PASS as distractor — reverses the roles of fundal massage and lower-segment support while retaining superficially plausible hand placement.
audit_findings.option_D: PASS as distractor — uterotonics and uterine massage are components of rapid first-response PPH treatment and are not intended to be sequenced by pausing massage until medication completion.
audit_findings.ambiguity: PASS — A is the only option matching the sourced technique and current first-response sequencing.
audit_findings.second_answer: EXCLUDED — B and C use incorrect mechanics; D incorrectly delays an immediate first-response intervention.
audit_findings.cueing: PASS — option lengths are closely matched and no absolute-word pattern or uniquely long keyed answer remains.
audit_findings.blueprint: PASS — NCSBN Physiological Adaptation explicitly includes care for pregnancy/labor/delivery complications such as hemorrhage and psychomotor care for body-system alterations.
audit_findings.independent_adversarial_second_pass: PASS — challenged whether uterotonic therapy should precede massage and whether alternate two-hand placements could be acceptable; WHO supports rapid concurrent first-response massage, while the NCBI technique specifically requires fundal massage with lower-segment support. A remains uniquely best.
